source.title: Compressed Computation under L⁴ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition

record.tranche_reason: It trains a toy network with a different objective and examines whether it shares computation across features and what geometry it learns. This conceptually tests superposition, but is not a reproduction of the original representation-model method.
record.gate_note: The post also reports results about reverse-engineering parameter values and comparing decomposition methods. Those are included only where they report the learned code geometry or its performance; citations to other studies are not treated as results here.
record.test_reason: The study trains a small ReLU network to compute 100 sparse features with 50 neurons, a compressed-computation task rather than the original representation task. It measures whether features share neurons through overlapping codewords and what geometry they take. This bears on V1 in a new setting. It sweeps the loss exponent but not sparsity or importance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that L⁴ (any exponent >2) training of the residual-free compressed-computation model elicits computation in superposition, whereas L² gives the naive solution. The mechanism is sparse near-biregular binary codewords decoded by a near-pseudoinverse, captured by three scalars at 1.13× loss. Hand-designed codes perform comparably, so the specific support is not special. Per-entry encoder values and residual decoder structure remain unexplained.
record.recipe_differences: This is a trained compressed-computation network, not a reproduction of the original toy representation model. It removes the residual connection, uses L⁴ rather than the usual L² objective, and presents an axis-aligned version; an embedded variant is also tested.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs between L² and exponents above 2. The smaller tested size gives weaker indications of superposition; the larger size gives a low coefficient of variation. The random embedding does not change the reported main results.

fits_no_version.finding: Computation in superposition (more nonlinear functions than neurons) arises in training only when the loss exponent exceeds 2. L² yields a naive non-superposed solution. The learned mechanism is a sparse binary code decoded by a near-pseudoinverse, resembling Hänni et al.'s constructions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained networks can compute in superposition via sparse binary codes over neurons, but whether this arises depends on the training objective (loss exponent).

record.problems: This is a narrow toy computation task. The text does not provide several numeric values because mathematical expressions are missing, including some loss-exponent results, codeword-degree statistics, size-sweep statistics, and attenuation slope. The smaller and larger size checks report only the loss statistic, not the full mechanism. Some figure results are summarized without exact values.

untested.parts: No sweep of feature sparsity or importance, so the sparsity-dependent phase transition is untested. The task is computing ReLUs rather than pure representation/reconstruction. Geometry is binary codewords rather than the polytope structures of the original. Larger and smaller sizes were checked only by the loss-spread statistic.

missing.what: Remaining Table 1 decompositions: free per-entry encoder with pinv 1.05×, 3 scalars with trained decoder 1.06×, decoder tied to pinv trained from scratch 1.05×. Also on-code values decrease with neuron degree, explaining part of the variance.
Author comment: much higher loss exponents give similar solutions with wider codeword-size spread, attributed to optimization failure.

record.verdict_notes: Many numbers in the source text are blank (stripped math), including the exponent-sweep CV range, codeword degree means, size-sweep CVs and attenuation slope. The study targets computation in superposition, a related construct. I link it to V1 because the hidden layer stores 100 features in 50 neurons via overlapping codewords. The L² null result concerns a computation task without importance weighting, so I treat it as a scope limit rather than a challenge.

versions.untested_parts: It does not sweep feature sparsity or feature importance, and its task is computing ReLUs rather than representing general features. It does not test the claim's broader sparsity-dependent transition or its applicability beyond these toy networks.
The study does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No LLM representations, neuron-level feature spread, or SAE recovery are tested.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are tested.
The study describes binary codewords across neurons but does not test whether represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional or multidimensional.
